based on their similarity to the original input.  Experimental results on the
Universal Dependencies and SemEval 2018 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of
the suggested approach.

We utilize the MESA-Black Hole code to investigate how post-merger jets are generated by a magnetized, rotating disk that forms following a binary neutron star collision. Our simulations, which involve magnetohydrodynamics and general relativity, as well as a simplified treatment of hyperon superfluids and neutrino cooling, reveal that a disk with an initial magnetic field of 10^10 G can produce an jet with a Poynting flux comparable to that generated by the accretion of the same field onto a black hole. We analyze the impact of various factors, including the spin rates of the binary components, on the jet production and find that a smaller initial magnetic field can still yield significant jets. We also investigate the effect of adding neutrino-cooled layers to the disk and observe that this can lead to the formation of hot spots that may be the source of short gamma-ray bursts.

Early-type galaxies are known to undergo frequent mergers and interactions, but this has historically been overlooked due to challenges in distinguishing between tidal features and the main body of galaxies when analyzing data. Recent studies have found that galaxy interactions and mergers are more prevalent than previously assumed, but it's unclear how common these events are in the broader early-type galaxy population. Our analysis of the data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Survey has revealed that tidal features and satellites constitute a significant portion of the light in early-type galaxies, amounting to approximately 10-15% of their total flux, and that these features and satellites are present in around 10-15% of all galaxies. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the majority of galaxies with massive satellites and interactions are concentrated in regions of high galaxy density. These results support the notion that galaxy interactions and interactions play a significant role in the formation and evolution of early-type galaxies.

A theoretical model developed in a previous study proposed that gravitons behave as massless particles with negative inertia, acting as the carriers of gravity. The present study further substantiates this model by providing observational evidence in the form of bipolar jets observed in various astrophysical settings. A complex arrangement of gravitational repulsion, in the vicinity of a central star, creates an unstable equilibrium that allows these jets to be emitted in opposite directions. The formation of these jets is attributed to the combined effects of the central star and the surrounding accretion disk, ultimately leading to the emission of bipolar outflows.

The origins of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) remain a significant challenge in astrophysics. By analyzing the polarization properties of FRBs, researchers aim to understand the role of neutron stars and black holes in generating these mysterious signals. A recent study of the FRB 20201115A, which has a regular pattern, revealed that FRBs do not exhibit radio or optical emissions simultaneously. Moreover, the analysis showed a lack of optical delay in the FRB 20201115A, setting a strict upper limit of 0.15 seconds. This finding provides new insights into the neutron star's magnetosphere, which is a leading theory for the FRB origin.

Designing a high-power laser system is a complex task that requires careful consideration of various factors, including thermal effects, beam pointing accuracy, damage thresholds, and more.  For existing laser systems, there's also a need to investigate potential performance limitations and areas for improvement, as well as exploring ways to upgrade the system to achieve higher output power.  This has led to the development of a new design tool called MAX-LASER, which is a comprehensive design tool for high-power laser systems.  In addition, a new reverse engineering tool has been developed to analyze and simulate high-power laser systems, allowing researchers to identify potential enhancements and optimize the system's performance.  This paper discusses the theoretical foundations and capabilities of these new tools, with a particular focus on the design and optimization of solid-state laser amplifiers, as well as the output coupling of the laser system.

Current language models excel at understanding and using language text, but fall short in scenarios requiring perception and reasoning. To bridge this gap, we propose integrating computer vision control into text generation for language models, enabling them to interact with visual environments. This approach, Language plus Control, leverages pre-trained vision and control models to produce text, similar to standard text generation. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we applied it to two challenging tasks: playing a 2D block-simulation game and solving a 2D physics puzzle. The results show that Language Model plus Control enables text-only models to interact with visual environments, and when used alone, also produces insightful visual and physical knowledge.

We present an innovative modification to the Cryptonite consensus algorithm,
which enhances transactional privacy within the blockchain framework. Our
solution, Delegated RingCT, features a substantially reduced data transfer
rate, which accelerates privacy-ensuring transactions. The enhanced
transactional performance is a result of the delegated data handling approach,
which assigns specific tasks to designated parties within the network, thus
alleviating the computational burden on individual miners.

Beam diagnostics is a critical aspect of accelerator physics that relies on measuring the behavior of charged particles within a beam. By using a detector to perform longitudinal and transverse scans of the beam's brightness, researchers can gather information about the beam's shape, current, and other characteristics. These measurements are particularly useful for analyzing the behavior of the beam as it propagates through the accelerator. In addition, these diagnostic tools can be applied to understand the properties of phase space distributions of any type.

A significant challenge in data-driven modeling is the discrepancy between a system's digital representation and the actual system it's designed to model. This paper explores how to reconcile this gap through collaborative data-driven modeling, focusing on leveraging the strengths of both human expertise and data. It examines ways to optimize this hybrid approach by developing methods to extract valuable information from data, train accurate models, and assess the reliability of data-driven models. Furthermore, the paper investigates the underlying dynamics of collaborative data-driven modeling and outlines strategies to optimize this process.

This research proposes that the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state, a molecular-like hybrid of $\Upsilon(1S)$ and $\rho$ particles, can transition into lighter $\Upsilon(nS)$ states and a pair of pions through a loop mechanism involving the $\rho$ particle. The loop mechanism also facilitates the observed rapid decays of $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^0$ states. Furthermore, by considering charge conjugation violating and isospin breaking effects caused by electromagnetic interactions and mass disparities between up and down quarks, the research predicts the amplitude of $\Upsilon(10753)$ transitioning into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$. The predicted amplitude is consistent with experimental data from the BESIII. The research also provides predictions for the branching ratios of $\Upsilon(10753)$ transitioning into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$, where n equals 1, 2, or 3, which can be tested by the Belle II.

This study introduces a novel optimization technique, quantized interval evolution (QIE), which evolves weight parameters within constrained intervals that dynamically adjust over time. QIE is designed to facilitate interval training of neural networks, paving the way for simultaneous network weight optimization and quantization. As a consequence of its constraints, QIE is mathematically analogous to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with stochastic interventions, yielding a QIE variant that mimics the effects of SGD, known as askew SGD, which is proven to be computationally efficient. Furthermore, the research presents an efficient implementation of QIE using tensor operations and demonstrates its efficacy on standard computer vision benchmarks, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet.

The past decade has witnessed significant advancements in Soft Robotics, particularly in the development of innovative design and modeling techniques. Researchers have successfully applied Soft Robotics in various practical settings, such as healthcare and industry. This article reviews the latest advancements in soft robotics control methods and highlights the most effective approaches. Moreover, it explores the effectiveness of a multi-disciplinary strategy, combining mechanical modeling and optimization, and outlines potential future research directions and challenges.

This study is about the Jacobi group in the context of the Jacobi-Lie theory. We are using a specific version of the Jacobi group which is essential in the Jacobi-Lie theory framework, and this genuine Jacobi group has been known for some time now. We are focusing on the Jacobi group's structure, composition series, and its connection to the modular group's subgroups.

Recent studies have shown that pre-trained language models can perform exceptionally well on Table fact verification tasks. However, the pre-trained models often rely on surface-level cues and may overlook the underlying structural and semantic connections in tables. In this study, we introduce the Explainer model, which leverages LLMs to pinpoint the most relevant table components and incorporate this information into an encoder-decoder architecture. The model's design allows it to effectively utilize pertinent table information, leading to improved performance on four low- and mid-resource Table fact verification datasets. Additionally, the model surpasses current state-of-the-explainability models in table fact verification tasks and offers more accurate and insightful table-based explanations than its competitors.

To improve the capabilities of image generation models, particularly in creating realistic, customized images, we've developed a novel approach that introduces an invisible layer of conditions within these models. Our method involves integrating a neural network that maps image features and novel condition inputs to accommodate site-specific and stylistic nuances. By combining this approach with standard untrained neural networks, we've effectively incorporated the natural variations within the image feature space and the condition space, resulting in a more versatile model capable of generating high-quality images from diverse datasets, such as the complex 'Chest X-ray' dataset.

The nested sampling method has been widely applied in Bayesian statistics, particularly in complex high-dimensional problems, to perform Bayesian evidence computation and posterior prediction under a constrained approach. Its core process involves iteratively accepting a set of samples that meet a step condition, and although theoretically justified, the step size significantly impacts computational efficiency. In this research, we analyze the performance of different step selectors, like a dynamic selector that adjusts the step size based on past acceptance rates, and compare them to established methods through a series of tests, including those in 2, 20, and 100 dimensions, and find that the adaptive selector can improve efficiency by up to two orders of magnitude.

For any connected graph, a fault-free distance labeling is a way to efficiently label vertices so that the distance between any two vertices can be determined within a certain multiplicative error margin, even if some intermediate vertices are damaged. Researchers have previously developed efficient distance labeling schemes for various graph types, but so far, no schemes have been proposed for planar graphs. In fact, a previous study proved that a certain class of general graphs cannot be efficiently labeled if more than a certain number of vertices are damaged. In contrast, we present a novel algorithm that can efficiently label n-vertex planar graphs, achieving optimal efficiency and minimizing potential damages. Specifically, our scheme can determine distances with an error margin that grows with the square root of n, and it can handle damages proportional to the square root of n, achieving this with a compact labeling size.

In this work, we examine the time and frequency domain relationships between two particles in a Bose-Hubbard model that is subject to external forces and loss of energy. Our investigation is carried out using the interaction picture, a quasi-exact method that allows us to calculate the model's propagator without making any assumptions. Two distinct types of correlations are analyzed: one that remains consistent over time and another that changes with time. We find that one type of correlation is primarily influenced by how the system begins, while the other is largely determined by how the system evolves. Additionally, we demonstrate that these correlations have distinct temporal and frequency range characteristics. Our research also reveals that the presence of energy loss leads to a broadening of the power spectrum and a decline in its overall intensity. Furthermore, we show that these effects are more pronounced in correlation types that change with time.

The authors establish a fundamental property for a specific category of elliptical equations expressed in divergence form, featuring coefficients representing currents on the half-space, with the coefficients' square values being bounded. A crucial estimate is derived, providing an estimate for weak solutions within the half-space, with currents' values being bounded by the gradient of solutions, resulting in an expression dependent on the currents, with an influence diminishing according to the formula $|y|^n$ as $y$ represents the coordinates in the half-space, with the coordinates $x$ representing the coordinates across the space. This estimate is subsequently utilized to demonstrate the continuous dependence of the solution with respect to the currents, with the authors also exploring how this estimate can be utilized to extend local regularity results from equations with coefficients representing currents in $L^q$, with $q>2$.

Recent research has demonstrated the potential of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection using Out-of-Distribution scores, which is highly effective in identifying data outside the training domain. One of the most successful methods for this purpose is Distribution Gaussian Processes (DGP). However, the current approach has a limitation in that it only detects OOD data that is completely outside the training domain. To overcome this issue, we introduce the concept of Distribution Gaussian Processes Strata (DG GP-Strata), which enables the detection of data that is not only outside the domain but also within it. By using the concept of density differences, our approach can effectively identify OOD data in various scenarios. Our results show that the proposed method is highly effective in both synthetic and real-world datasets, such as CIFAR10 and ImageNet, and it is also available in an open-source code repository.

In the realm of non-equilibrium quantum systems, understanding the phenomenon of high-energy condensation is a significant challenge. Our research demonstrates that in an open, non-integrable lattice system with dissipative effects, the introduction of noise can actually enhance system condensation. Specifically, we utilize a multi-site Floquet Hamiltonian with a specific 'scar-like' eigenstate, which under a dynamical transformation leads to a many-body Fock state. By applying a dephasing noise model, we show that it can effectively suppress the Scarce excitation and promote system condensation. Moreover, we reveal that the rate of condensation is contingent upon the frequency of periodic driving, which can be leveraged to manipulate the system's behavior. Our findings suggest that they can be realized experimentally using optical lattices and ultracold atoms.

Research has shown that several partial differential equations, including the Monge--Amp\`ere equation, have connections to Alexandrov maximum principles and H\"older continuous functions for their solutions. Specifically, studies have found that their solutions exhibit H\"older continuous properties with respect to the Hessian's inverse square, the distance between points in the space, and functions with square integrable distributions. This paper builds on these findings by expanding the Alexandrov maximum principles to a broader range of nonlinear elliptic equations, encompassing a notable improvement for the Monge--Amp\`ere equation when its right-hand side is bounded. A notable consequence of this research is that the H\"older continuous properties of its solutions can be improved to H^1, where H is any real number greater than or equal to 1/2.

In the study of complex quantum systems, statistical analysis of 'optical clocks' is crucial. The local and temporal order parameters derived from measurements provide insights into the underlying quantum dynamics. The 'clock skewness' and 'clock kurtosis' are defined as higher-order order parameters that measure the order within time-resolved intensity distributions. The paper investigates the local and temporal distributions of clock skewness and kurtosis in a three-level system, using quantum trajectories in a driven-dissipative framework. The study focuses on 'open quantum clocks' where both kurtosis and skewness exhibit non-trivial behavior. The temporal evolution of these parameters shows complex patterns, including transitions between chaos and coherence, which are influenced by local and temporal dynamics. The phase space structure and order parameter behavior are also examined, revealing local and temporal symmetries. The study highlights the connection between order parameters and quantum dynamics, offering a deeper understanding of complex quantum systems.

This study addresses Service Function Chaining (SFC) disruptions within Software Defined Networks (SDN) by introducing an innovative fog-assisted restoration strategy. Focusing on real-time SFCs, which necessate strict time constraints, we develop a comprehensive fog-supported SFC restoration approach to ensure rapid service delivery. Notably, our strategy not only addresses network service failures but also considers failure prevention. Failing to account for real-time SFCs' time sensitivity could result in increased network load, leading to service failure. Our proposed fog-assisted strategy involves Joint Failure Restoration and Fault Prevention (JFRFP), a comprehensive solution to ensure efficient service delivery. This involves optimizing energy-efficient resources within the network, represented as Integer Linear Programming (JFRFP) optimization problem, and subsequently, devising a heuristic algorithm to solve the optimization problem. Simulation results indicate that our proposed JFRFP solution outperforms existing SFC restoration methods in terms of successful service delivery and efficient resource utilization.

The choice of loss function is a pivotal decision in neural network design,
significantly influencing the optimization process. Unfortunately, there's
often a lack of clear understanding about the loss function's role, leading to
experimentation with trial and error. In this study, we provide a systematic
examination of the impact loss functions have on the loss and gradient values
during training. By applying a technique known as gradient surgery, we can
isolate and analyze the effects of individual loss functions. Our analysis
involves investigating four key properties of these functions: (i) their effect
on the magnitude of gradients, (ii) their contribution to model accuracy, (iii)
their ability to maintain class balance, and (iv) their influence on generalization.
Through this research, we provide insights into selecting suitable loss functions
for specific tasks and model objectives.

We developed the Hyper-InERA, a new class of holographic quantum error correction codes that can accurately model systems exhibiting power-law patterns. The code combines power-law entanglement between the code's distance and bond-dimension with a scalable classical efficiency and a decaying error rate based on bond-dimension. For large distances, the corrected error is approximately proportional to $(1/2)^{b^{\alpha}}$, surpassing the standard linear error pattern and enabling long-range interactions in quantum systems. The Hyper-INERA code is derived from a modified tensor network architecture based on the AdS/CFT correspondence, incorporating a tensor network renormalization procedure to confirm its effectiveness.

The population of filaments in the Galactic Center, visible in both CO and radio emissions, has been known for decades. Recent research revealed that these filaments are not evenly spread out but instead clustered together, pointing to a possible common origin. We hypothesize that the filaments along the Galactic Plane originate from the same population and originated from the same source. By analyzing the spacing between filaments, we found that the distances follow a distribution that is consistent with our hypothesis. We also observed a pattern in which filaments are more densely packed as we move along the Galactic Plane, indicating a possible relationship with the Galactic Plane's density. We found that the density of filaments is influenced by both random placement and by their tendency to be positioned in areas with higher density. We also discovered that the filaments are not evenly spread out in the Galactic Plane, but instead tend to be positioned in areas with higher density. We also discovered that the filaments are not evenly spread out in the Galactic Plane, but instead tend to be positioned in areas with higher density.

This research introduces a new method for reducing energy consumption in smart distribution grids through demand-side management. The proposed technique, Conservation Voltage Decrease, involves centrally managed, secondary-level voltage reductions that result in substantial load reductions. Our objective is to optimize DE within a hierarchical system, incorporating DE in the primary and DSGs in the secondary, and considers the interaction between these components. The DE problem is formulated as a two-level optimization problem, consisting of a quadratic master problem and a linear slave problem. To facilitate decentralized solution methods for both problems, a distributed algorithm is developed, which enables DE in both the primary and secondary systems while ensuring finite convergence to the optimal solution. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through numerical examples.

In the context of nonstochastic bandits and advisors, we investigate the impact of various types of communication lags on system performance. The system involves an nonstochastic bandit expert who receives delayed feedback for each arm, and both the bandit and advisors operate over infinite time horizons. In the case of logarithmic losses, we introduce a no-regret algorithm under specific conditions regarding the problem's geometry, demonstrating logarithmic regret in the bandit setting and a constant factor improvement in the expert setting compared to systems without delays. For systems using square losses, we prove a lower bound on regret that increases exponentially with delay, illustrating that logarithmic losses are more resilient to communication lags. Furthermore, we show that similar results can be achieved with arm-independent linear losses, offering constant regret in the expert setting and $\tilde{O}(e^{d^*})$ regret in the bandit setting, where $d^*$ represents the maximum delay.

This paper presents LEATHER, a text-based learning framework specifically designed for creating authentic dialogue within human-like contexts. LEATHER is built on an abstract model of text generation, incorporating a knowledge representation and learning to text (LT) model. The 'Human Knowledge and Text Model' (HKTM) was created to simulate human knowledge and text generation processes. HKTM is composed of a Human Knowledge Model (HKM) and a Knowledge Text Model (KTM). The HKM is a fact graph augmented with semantic relationships, while the KTM is a neural network that generates fluent text. LEATHER learns to create knowledge and text that mimic human counterparts. The proposed framework was tested using three datasets: SNLI, SNLI-SN, and SNLI-RG, which evaluate the human-likeness of text generated by machines. The results demonstrate that LEATHER can create knowledge and text that are significantly more human-like than existing LT models.

This article examines the quantum chromodynamics on a lattice when there's a finite temperature and density, with a focus on theoretical background and current findings. Additionally, an appendix provides an overview of the Nambu--Jona-Lasinio model on a finite thermal circle.

A key component of reducing costs in offshore wind energy production lies in minimizing the expense of gathering critical data through site surveys, particularly local wind speed and turbulence measurements. Analyzing long-term wind data can be challenging due to the sheer volume of information. To overcome this, researchers have developed a Gaussian Process regression technique for efficiently extracting meaningful insights from extended time series. This approach enables the creation of a comprehensive stress prediction model for offshore wind turbines, incorporating uncertainty estimates, which in turn facilitates the detection of anomalous readings during the site survey phase.

Natural disasters such as earthquakes can cause significant destruction and loss of life, 
leaving victims with immense trauma and emotional distress. Social media has become a powerful tool 
for disseminating real-time information and providing a platform for individuals to express their 
grief and seek emotional support. This research investigates the utility of social media in the context 
of natural disasters by analyzing Twitter data related to the 2023 Mozlaarhinde earthquake in Turkey. 
Using the Python Twitter API, tweets were collected and a comprehensive network was developed, allowing 
for the exploration of its structural and semantic properties. The results demonstrate the potential 
of social media in facilitating information sharing and emotional support among disaster survivors.

A group exhibits property $R_\infty$ when its Alexander polynomial has infinite reduced twisted fixed points under the Reynolds operator in the case of the infinite dihedral action. This paper delves into the $R_\infty$ property in relation to certain groups derived from Baumslag-Solitar groups and shows that variations of these groups, as well as their nilpotent extensions, retain property $R_\infty$. Additionally, the study provides updated insights on the $R_\infty$ property for the original groups and their extensions.

A new method for inverting time-resolved data has been developed within a trajectory basis framework. This approach formulates the inversion process as a continuous optimization problem, where the objective function is convex and can be efficiently solved. Unlike conventional methods that rely on a predefined model structure, this algorithm makes no such assumptions. Instead, it optimizes a set of non-negative trajectory weights. Notably, these weights remain model-agnostic and can be applied to various inverse problems, such as reconstructing quantum states or analyzing time-dependent spectra. The method's efficacy has been demonstrated through both simulated and experimental data analysis.

Naturalistic Driving Studies utilize real-world driving footage to examine the complexities of real-world driving scenarios. However, existing datasets are limited in scope, hindering research across multiple domains. This research presents a comprehensive naturalistic driving dataset, referred to as SceNDD, which encompasses a variety of scenarios including traffic regulations, road rules, and regulations specific to certain regions. The dataset consists of 1,000 video clips, each featuring a driver and multiple passengers, with annotations for steering angles, vehicle speed, and the number of occupants. A significant finding reveals that existing methods for automatic annotation are unreliable in this context. To address this challenge, a novel automatic annotation system utilizing a combination of computer vision and driver profiling techniques is proposed. The research further discusses the ethical considerations and driving scenarios captured within the SceNDD, along with the research community's response to the release of the dataset.

In this context, we explore an extension of the boundary conformal field theory to include one-dimensional interfaces, a concept that can be related to phase transitions in 3D systems. Our analysis involves examining the thermal properties of the boundary field in relation to the boundary's presence, a relationship that can be attributed to topological entanglement. Building upon this relationship, we introduce the reflected entropy as a measure of entanglement pertinent to the boundary, and subsequently, we derive the mutual information in the context of one-dimensional radial intervals. Our findings are further substantiated by the application of the boundary/interface state model of the Ramond sector.

Recent research has highlighted the potential of reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to improve wireless communication systems. A novel model, which incorporates the smart surface in the access link, has been proposed to enhance performance. A deep learning approach, specifically a variant of the Extreme Learning Machine, has been developed to efficiently estimate the communication channel. A modified version of the smart surface, which uses sub-carriers instead of antennas for higher spectral efficiency, has been proposed. A deep learning method, which processes the smart surface's phase shifts and the receiver's signal, has been shown to accurately estimate the channel's impulse response, even in the presence of limited cyclic prefix data. A theoretical analysis of the proposed model has been provided, and simulation results have demonstrated its effectiveness and robustness.

One key principle of quantum mechanics is the measurement postulate, which states that measurements inherently cause the wave function to collapse. A recently discovered theorem called Integral Variation, derived from measuring a single energy value, reveals that wave function collapse is a result of this measurement. Integral Variation is achieved by summing the log ratios of the measured wave function before and after the process. This measurement need not be projective. The Integral Variation theorem provides an objective measure of the energy wave function's change. It has also been demonstrated that energy measurements can be used to detect projective measurements. This measurement can be used to detect non-projective measurements with high precision, making it a valuable tool for studying the quantum-classical boundary.

We are examining the deformation conditions for G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A key finding is that the deformation space of a compact, stable G2-instanton is inherently finite-dimensional. Moreover, we are investigating the limiting behavior of the deformation space as the nearly G2-geometry converges to a truly G2-geometry. The relationship between these two scenarios is quantified by bounds that depend on the geometry's structure constant. This result has a direct implication: the convergence of a sequence of G2-instantons on nearly G2-geometries results in a limit that constitutes a critical point of the Yang-Mills functional on the limiting G2-geometry.

COVID-19 has had a significant impact on the world, with the most striking consequence being the loss of over 3 million lives.  To contain the spread, countries have adopted contact tracing as a key strategy, employing various technologies to scale up.  One effective method is the use of proximity detection systems, which can be seamlessly integrated into contact tracing apps.  This paper focuses on an Android-based app, demonstrating its implementation, data flow, and privacy features.  We highlight the app's adherence to the Swiss contact tracing system, emphasizing its focus on protecting user information.  By outlining the system's architecture, we show how an Android app can be developed to align with a contact tracing framework, ensuring that proximity data is only processed by a trusted authority.  This paper serves as a starting point for developing contact tracing apps that prioritize user privacy.

Neural systems are highly regarded for their exceptional computational and memory capabilities. Notably, the human brain alone can process approximately 1 petabyte per second of data and store up to 1 yottabyte of information. Notable characteristics of neural computation include parallel processing, content-addressable memory, and sparse connectivity. These features bear resemblance to key principles in quantum information, leading researchers to speculate about potential quantum properties in neural systems. This study delves into the existing quantum brain hypothesis and its underpinning theories, including coherence and entanglement, to assess the likelihood of a neural system functioning as a quantum computer. Additionally, the potential benefits of quantum neural systems are examined, with a notable advantage being the ability to efficiently solve complex optimization problems through adiabatic quantum computing.

A newly proven theorem allows for a direct incorporation of ACL2 within itself and this concept has been utilized to create an ACL2 based tool for generating C code, which also incorporates the ACL2 proof checker.  This innovative C code creator, named ACL2C, was designed to address some of the complexities inherent in existing C proof tools, such as GCC and Clang, which can be cumbersome to utilize.  By leveraging the simplicity of shallow embedding, ACL2C circumvents some of these difficulties and streamlines the process of incorporating C functionality into the theorem prover.  Furthermore, it enables the creation of more precise abstractions and more sophisticated proof techniques when compared to other C proof tools.  This paper outlines the principles behind this approach and showcases several practical applications of ACL2C.

Precise measurements of asteroid Iochroma's orbital elements are available from JPL's Deep Space Network Horizons, specifically its semimajor axis, eccentricity, and mean anomaly. Analyzing these data through both numerical integrations and linear approximations, we find that Iochroma's orbit is influenced by Iapetus and Laplace's 3:2 mean motion resonance. The numerical model predicts that JPL's data will match Iochroma's current position in the resonance by the year 2100. The long-term evolution of Iochroma's eccentricity is also affected by the Kozai mechanism and general relativistic effects.

Building upon the relationship between Ramanujan's zeta values and the Hurwitz zeta functions, we express the odd zeta values in terms of the Hurwitz zeta functions and their derivatives, adhering to Ramachandra's specified format of the zeta functions and their differentiation orders.

We establish that the logical circle-equivariant elliptic cohomology ring of complex projective space $CP(V)$, where $V$ is a finite-dimensional $C^{\infty}$-vector bundle, is the elliptic Hopf algebra elliptic elliptic Hopf algebra equivariant elliptic cohomology of the elliptic curve $T$, is isomorphic to.

We have developed a physics-informed machine learning approach that utilizes manifold learning and neural networks to address challenges in algebraic topology. Specifically, neural networks are trained to recognize properties of a given data manifold, with their loss functions incorporating physical laws. By optimizing these networks, we can obtain a high-quality embedding that adheres to both the data manifold structure and physical constraints. This method is demonstrated through its application to discovering and solving equations that describe phenomena such as fluid dynamics and heat transfer.

This research undertakes a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the distribution patterns of $J/\psi$ in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions at 10.6 GeV. The investigation primarily focuses on the $J/\psi$ production in association with $\eta_c$ and the $J/\psi$ production in association with $\chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) processes. The study reveals that at this energy level, the $s$- and $d$-wave polarization of $J/\psi$ in the $J/\psi+\eta_c$ reaction are roughly equal, while in the $J/\psi+\chi_{c0},\chi_{c1},\chi_{c2}$ reactions, $s$-wave dominates. The $q^2$ distribution of $J/\psi$ in the $J/\psi+\eta_c$ reaction is found to be relatively flat, whereas in the $J/\psi+\chi_{c0},\chi_{c1},\chi_{c2}$ reactions, $q^2$ is concentrated at low values. The $q^2$ distribution serves as a crucial indicator for distinguishing between $J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$ reactions.

Our online survey examined 100 signal users' knowledge of the service's 6-digit PIN, focusing on their understanding of the feature's purpose and the implications of the PIN's characteristics. The results showed that users were largely unaware of the PIN's security-related function and the implications of the following: whether the PIN feature can be turned off, whether existing chats remain accessible after changing the PIN, whether deleting a contact also removes access to the chat, and whether the chat can be accessed after account deletion. The study's findings have significant implications for users' awareness of the signal security policy.

To determine the average power of a solar energy generator, the time interval over which the sun shines must be calculated. The solar elevation angle is typically defined by two boundaries: one at sunrise and the other at sunset. By integrating the square of this angle, the mean solar power can be found. The boundaries of integration are actually determined by specific values of solar irradiation, which can be approximated by Gaussian quadrature. However, this method is only effective if weights are determined by solar elevation cosine values. Unfortunately, this leads to complex expressions for the roots and weights of the polynomial, which are difficult to calculate. A new approach involves a transformation of solar power into solar elevation, which simplifies the problem. This method has been tested with sample times and roots and weights for four typical scenarios.

The curvature of the loss landscape is characterized by the Hessian matrix, which in deep learning applications is typically approximated through stochastic methods such as Hessian sketch or Hessian-vector products. These stochastic approaches, however, fail to directly capture the underlying curvature. In contrast, our proposed method involves utilizing the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, which can be efficiently low-rank compressed, thereby providing a precise characterization of the loss landscape structure. By leveraging this approach, we are able to solve the compressed system exactly, thereby offering insights into the loss landscape curvature. This approach further enables the development of an enhanced stochastic optimization algorithm, which converges at the rate of the state-of-the-art deterministic methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

This study examines the impact of grammatical gender on language processing,
focusing on German as a representative gender-marking language. We demonstrate
that German speakers' gender associations with nouns influence their word-in
word relationships, measured through EEG-ERP components. ERP data analysis
reveals that gender-related processing occurs within 250ms after noun processing,
indicating that gender associations significantly impact how speakers represent
words in real-time. Furthermore, our findings suggest that gender influences
not only the representation of the initial noun but also the underlying verb
representation, bolstered by support from a computational model. These results
imply that gender associations in German profoundly affect the representation
of the entire sentence, offering new insights into the interplay between lexical
features and sentence processing.

In the context of variations of Shimura data (r, X, R, C), a subgroup r^+ of r is defined as r^+ = ker(w), where w represents the complex conjugation automorphism. It is assumed that r^+ has a rank that is at least one-half of the rank of r. A subgroup Gamma of r^+(C) is said to be k-stiff, where k is a non-zero integer, if the index of the subgroup r^+ intersect Gamma in r^+ is at least a quadratic function of Gamma, specifically, the index is greater than or equal to c times the absolute value of k, where c is the corank of r^+. Examples are given demonstrating that such stiff classes exist for k.

Estimating an object's 3D position is a crucial aspect of many computer vision tasks, such as autonomous driving and robotic manipulation. However, most approaches rely on precise 2D detection or assume training data includes objects from various contexts and orientations. This work tackles the challenge of detecting objects without prior knowledge of their appearance or 3D position, by proposing a method that uses image-level information to estimate object locations. This method generates object proposals based on the appearance of detected objects, which is then used to train a position estimator. Through extensive experiments, the proposed approach shows that it can accurately estimate 3D object locations after being trained only on a small number of object instances from a single category, while also outperforming a method that uses 3D object proposals.

Traffic forecasting is a crucial aspect of intelligent transportation systems.
However, conventional methods are often hindered by limited data and limited features.
To overcome these limitations, this research proposes a novel approach that uses
similarities between road sections to gather and share data across different road
sections.
The new method is called the Similarity-based Attribute Extraction (S.A.E.) model.
It enhances the forecasting model by incorporating additional attributes derived
from the road network, such as the similarity between road sections, and by using
the combined information from multiple related road sections.
The proposed S.A.E. model, along with the results of the study, are available for
public use on the GitHub platform.

This study introduces VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders that enables efficient handling of large-scale interventional and counterfactual inquiries in complex networks. By leveraging the properties of latent variable models, the VACA framework provides a clear connection between interventional distribution and model parameters. As such, the encoders in VACA can be trained using maximum likelihood estimation based on observational data, allowing for accurate estimation of intervention and counterfactual outcomes. Furthermore, the analysis shows that VACA's behavior under interventional inquiries is largely unaffected by its variational limitations. As such, VACA can be viewed as a practical and reliable solution for large interventional counterfactual inquiries, particularly in cases where the true model is complex and difficult to work with directly.

In this paper, we introduce the First Light results of the transient acquisition system, REALTA, which is part of the LOFAR array's infrastructure. This system, installed at LOFAR's Irish station in 2021, enables the REALTA to rapidly detect and locate transient radio sources within a few milliseconds. With the capability to pinpoint these transients with sub-degree resolution, the system triggers the acquisition of high-resolution data within a few seconds. Demonstrating the capabilities of REALTA, we present a study on 1.5 hours of data collected within the 140-240 MHz frequency band, which revealed 10 transients. These transients, which have flux densities of at least 0.1 Jy, were found to possess time-scales of at least 10 milliseconds. Additionally, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the transient detection system and its ability to accurately reconstruct the positions of transients. Furthermore, the study showcases the ability of the system to identify transients with high spectral resolution, which is demonstrated through the analysis of a few selected transients.

A thorough examination of the interplay between machine learning and metaphotonics is presented. Metaphotonics, utilizing photons as a functional unit, harnesses machine learning to achieve advancements in optical computing, optimization, and sensing. Our research outlines the fundamental principles of metaphotonics and highlights its key applications. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of metaphotonics underpinned by machine learning is provided, covering supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, and graph theory. A comprehensive review of recent research in this area, discussing both its current capabilities and challenges, is presented.

This research undertakes a comprehensive data analysis of the comprehensive IMDb dataset.
Conventional movie data sets typically encompass basic information, such as release year, director, lead actors, and box office earnings.
However, an established dataset is limited in scope, lacking key attributes that influence a movie's commercial success.
To address this, an expanded dataset has been developed, including pre-release attributes that can be leveraged for predictive modeling.
Utilizing the enhanced dataset, movie data has been further categorized into distinct director and genre groups.
By applying a data-driven approach, this research investigates the impact of pre-release attributes on potential commercial performance.
The findings indicate that attributes such as star power, movie rating, and genre have a substantial effect on a movie's final earnings.
A random forest model has been employed to analyze the relationship between pre-release attributes and commercial success.
The results of the analysis reveal that attributes such as lead actors and initial movie ratings are critical factors in determining a movie's ultimate financial outcome.

This work examines the intersection of two key variables - frequency and node voltage - within the power grid, focusing on its dynamic behavior. The research identifies two primary mechanisms for stabilizing grid behavior: alternative frequency control and secondary control, each playing a distinct yet interconnected role. To analyze these control methods, the study develops a novel mathematical model, combining detailed bus dynamics with a sub-transient voltage representation. By incorporating the effects of grid inductance and resistance, the work creates a unified mathematical framework governing node voltages and grid frequency. Through this model, the researchers demonstrate how secondary control influences frequency dynamics, while also exploring how the power grid's resistive nature impacts the dynamic behavior of voltages and frequency.

The fusion of cyber systems with physical systems has created networks called cyber-physical networks (CPNs) that are used in a wide range of applications, such as controlling complex systems, gathering data, and tracking information. To manage the growing complexity of CPNs, researchers are exploring the potential of incorporating intelligent elements into their design. This paper outlines the theoretical framework for enhancing CPNs with intelligence by employing machine learning and data analytics. By examining the characteristics of CPNs, this research aims to identify areas where intelligent enhancements can be applied to improve the performance and efficiency of these networks. To support this goal, the paper also provides a catalog of relevant cyber technologies that can be used to implement intelligent components within CPNs.

Blazars, a class of active galactic nuclei, are known for their variable, polarized electromagnetic radiation, which peaks in the radio to X-ray spectrum.  This type of blazar exhibits significant and variable polarization in all wavelengths, which is puzzling in the framework of the standard two-zone blazar model.  This model suggests that the X-rays are produced by the inverse Compton scattering of X-ray synchrotron radiation from polarized radio emission, which should result in polarized X-rays.  However, observations of some blazars have shown unpolarized X-rays, contradicting the standard two-zone blazar model.  This study investigates the impact of instrumental and astrophysical factors on polarization measurements using Monte-Carlo simulations.  This work, titled Utilization to the UV/Soft X-ray Excess in Blazar Spectra as a Testbed for Polarization Measurement Analysis, reveals that instrumental effects and astrophysical processes can significantly affect polarization measurements, which may explain the unpolarized X-rays observed in some blazars.

We investigate the implications of extending the parameters of multivariate functions into the complex domain for fitting real data points. Our research reveals that certain complex parameter configurations, like those found in the tangential plane to a real parameter surface, can yield superior model performance compared to purely real parameters. We observe that a small adjustment in the imaginary component of one parameter can significantly enhance the model's likelihood. Furthermore, the introduction of a non-zero imaginary part to another parameter can result in substantial improvements to the model's fit. We also explore the parameter dependence of the log likelihood for a specific cosmological model, specifically the Planck likelihood, and discover that introducing complex dimensions to some parameters can yield improved fits. Our analysis indicates that extending parameters into the complex domain is a valuable tool for optimizing model fits and can be applied to various real data sets.

This research explores the problem of identifying and recognizing pure quantum states that have the same symmetry properties. Specifically, we're examining a scenario where an observer receives a stream of identically prepared quantum states and aims to determine the state's identity after a fixed number of measurements. Our focus is on understanding how the underlying symmetry of quantum states affects the observer's ability to distinguish between them. By analyzing this problem using large deviation theory, we're examining the error rates associated with different measurement strategies and finding that the speed at which these rates decrease depends on the square of the distance between the states in a specific geometric space that accounts for their symmetry properties. Our results also reveal that, in certain cases, no matter how many measurements are made, the observer can only achieve a certain level of accuracy, influenced by a specific angle related to the states' orientation within a specific framework.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on a QCD string with a twisted structure. Baryon-antibaryon pairs are produced through a fragmentation process that follows the dynamics of a fermion moving along a quantized, twister QCD string. This model naturally explains Baryon number conservation, as well as various properties of baryon-meson correlations, including meson momentum related to Baryon spin. It also offers a clear understanding of baryon magnetic moments, which can be directly linked to the properties of the QCD string itself.

The Sun's north-south travel time difference in p-modes is a key indicator of its internal meridional flow. To understand the travel time's contribution from currents near active regions, we analyzed data from HMI and SO/MDI for a sample of 1200 regions over a 10-year period. We found that these currents cause time-averaged phase shifts of approximately 0.05 seconds, primarily due to their widespread distribution and relatively low average speed. This effect is significant, but it does not show a preference for northern or southern hemispheres. Additionally, we found that the travel time's dependence on solar frequency is minimal, with an average of 0.002 seconds per megahertz.

Gravitational waves generated by magnetic fields created during the inflation period can solve long-standing cosmological problems.  However, researchers have been divided over whether these waves leave detectable imprints in certain frequency ranges.  In this study, we investigate the spectrum of GWs created by magnetic fields within the frequency range of the Pulsar Timing Array and find that previous models underestimated the GW spectrum.  Our analysis reveals that the energy transferred to the universe through magnetic fields is primarily determined by two key factors: the amplitude of magnetic fields observed today and the magnetic fields' behavior during the epoch between inflation and radiation domination.  If magnetic fields were created through a specific process called magnetic reconnection, we predict that GWs from this phenomenon will produce significant signals detectable by Pulsar Timing Array.  These signals are expected to have characteristic features that can be distinguished from other detectable sources.

The increasing popularity of 4K light field displays and the subsequent rise in data requirements necessitate the use of efficient compression techniques. In response to this, a novel, data-driven compression method is presented. Unlike traditional methods, this approach employs a context-aware neural network to generate an optimized lossy compression, thereby optimizing the network's performance in terms of its rate-distortion trade-off. The experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms existing techniques, achieving improvements of up to 1.5 dB. Moreover, this method facilitates lossless image reconstruction with high fidelity.

Achieving cross-lingual information retrieval without requiring training data is a significant challenge. Bilingual vector models offer a promising solution, but they often require substantial training data and substantial computational resources. To overcome these limitations, we explore combining interactive and non-interactive models to leverage multiple models' capabilities. Our proposed approach involves fusing the cross-lingual representations from both models to enhance performance. Experimental results on various benchmarks demonstrate that our method surpasses existing approaches, including simple ensembling methods, and achieves state-of-the-art outcomes on several key metrics.

This study compares design-based model-based techniques for improving small-area estimates in countries with low to middle income levels. A survey was conducted using a two-stage sampling method in 18 of 19 provinces in Guatemala, collecting data from 1,100 households regarding food security status. The results, obtained from GuateAsegura, were analyzed using a series of models, including Markov chains, to identify factors influencing province-level food security. The analysis revealed that economic conditions, including GDP and exchange rates, significantly impact food security status. The study also found that economic growth and depreciation of local currencies are associated with improved food security. The economic and political contexts of Guatemala, including its reliance on external currencies, were significant factors in determining its level of food security. The analysis of variance revealed that 60.5% of the variation in food security could be attributed to economic factors, while 39.5% was unexplained. The model-based approach demonstrated good predictive accuracy, with 70% of the variance in estimates within 5% of their true values. The results suggest that economic indicators can be used to develop predictive models of small-area estimates, which could be useful for policy-making and resource allocation.

The concept of Kelly wagers is widely used in financial markets to optimize profit, and can also be applied in information theory. However, traditional methods are limited to discrete systems, and our study introduces a approach using straddle options to deal with continuous systems, and it is demonstrated that our method converges to the optimal Kelly wagers in large pay-off scenarios.

The excitonic properties of the recently discovered two-dimensional monolayer compounds, consisting of group 6 and group 14 elements, have been investigated using a first-principles approach. By analyzing the quasiparticle electronic structures and optical properties, researchers discovered that in most compounds, a stack-independent exciton is present, except for GP$_2$. Furthermore, it was found that in MP$_2$ and MW$_4$, the band arrangement significantly influences the quasiparticle optical spectrum. These findings indicate that the band arrangement is a crucial factor in determining the optical properties of these compounds.

The study of rare decays of heavy flavor hadrons can provide valuable insights into physics beyond the Standard Model. One such process is the radiative decay of a $\Sigma^+$ baryon into a proton and a lepton pair, specifically $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. Utilizing data collected by the LHCb experiment between 2011 and 2018, researchers observed this decay for the first time. A statistical significance of $7.4\sigma$ was achieved, and measurements were made for both the $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma \gamma$ and $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching fractions. Additionally, form factors describing these decays were determined and found to be consistent with theoretical predictions.

A comprehensive analysis of a sample of Taurus Basiachs objects revealed the presence of distinct molecular signatures, including CO and SiO, indicating the presence of CO and shock activity within the sources. Utilizing the ALMA observations, researchers examined the spatial distribution of these molecular components and found that sources with distinct spatial patterns of these molecules are likely to host Basiachs objects. A theoretical model of Basiachs object formation, incorporating a rotating protoplanetary disk, predicted the presence of a distinct spatial pattern of CO emission, which matched the observed sources. Furthermore, the model suggested that a significant portion of Basiachs objects are in the process of accretion, and that a significant mass of the Basiachs objects is concentrated in the central region.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are distorted by the Earth's atmosphere's varying refractive index, causing chromatic image displacement and distortion. To address this, special optical devices, known as atmospheric dispersion correctors, are required. During the past decade, the ATLAS collaboration has conducted extensive field tests, collecting comprehensive data on the atmosphere's distortions. This paper outlines the mathematical models used to interpret these measurements, which are crucial for predicting the performance of ADCs and evaluating the atmosphere's dispersion based on telescope azimuth and elevation readings. Three models are proposed: the empirical model, which relies on empirical relations, the physical model, which uses a combination of temperature and refractivity, and the hybrid model, which combines elements of both. Each model demonstrates satisfactory agreement with measured values, with the hybrid model offering the best results.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian method for handling multi-period time series data, which often consists of irregular intervals and missing values. Our approach employs Bayesian modeling, leveraging the natural fit for irreregularities in order to fill in missing time points. To handle the high dimensionality of multi-period data, we incorporate a unique sparse and group-lasso prior for the state-space model parameters. This prior enables the automatic selection of significant features while also improving the model's ability to handle large datasets. To obtain the posterior distribution of the model, we employ a variational inference technique, which approximates the distribution by integrating out the latent states. This approach is particularly efficient, as it can process data across multiple time periods. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through its application to real-world multi-period temperature data, where we analyze and compare its performance with existing alternatives.

This note establishes a connection between Pontryagin duality for locally compact abelian groups and Solvability Rank Properties in constant first-order logic. The primary outcome shows that the topological dual of a locally compact abelian group can be expressed using a countable group given a specific topology. The text also provides an example of an abelian group for which no explicit formula can be found that describes its topology, highlighting the limitations of Pontryagin duality in the context of constant logic.

This work investigates how to address fairness issues in Federated Learning (FL) when considering both local data equity and model fairness. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between fairness and differential privacy (DP) within the context of Federated Learning. To achieve these goals, we first establish fairness definitions for FL, local and global. Subsequently, we explore methods for incorporating fairness into FL, such as re-sampling and constraint-based approaches. Next, we delve into how FL and DP intersect, specifically focusing on model fairness and DP joint satisfaction. Key findings include model robustness under both fairness and DP, and the existence of information-theoretic limits to achieving both objectives. Lastly, how FL and DP interact with fairness is explored, with open questions raised for future research.

A supersymmetric version of the basic $U(1)_X$ model is considered, incorporating a right-handed neutrino field as the dark energy source. The model features two Higgs doublets and one Higgs triplet that interact with the $U(1)_X$ field, including two right-handed neutrinos that have Majorana masses. The model's superpotential is modified by nonrenormalizable operators that arise from high-energy physics. The model is analyzed with respect to its low-energy spectrum, electroweak symmetry breaking, and dark matter. The model's implications for dark energy are explored, including a relationship between the dark energy scale and the $U(1)_X$ field's right-handed neutrino field. The model's low-energy spectrum is consistent with the existence of a right-handed neutrino field, which has a mass on the order of the electroweak scale. The model's implications for dark matter are explored, including the possibility that the $U(1)_X$ field's right-handed neutrino field is the source of dark energy. The model's implications for low-energy physics are explored, including the possibility that the $U(1)_X$ field's right-handed neutrino field has a mass on the order of the electroweak scale. The model's implications for dark energy are explored, including the possibility that the $U(1)_X$ field's right-handed neutrino field has a mass on the order of the electrow

In a wireless-powered network assisted by intelligent surfaces and experiencing interference, we've developed a deep unsupervised learning method for optimizing the reflection coefficients. The method aims to maximize the network's throughput while ensuring all devices receive sufficient energy. The proposed approach consists of two key components: a master network responsible for energy transfer and a slave network responsible for data transmission. The master network is trained to transfer energy efficiently to the slaves, while the slave network is trained to generate optimal coefficients that maximize network throughput and ensure energy availability. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through simulation results, which show significant performance improvements.

For the first time, researchers have observed the $\beta$-decay of $^{186}$Hg, which has a half-life of 2.68 milliseconds. The half-life of the $^{186}$Hg isomer has been measured at 1.91 milliseconds. The $\beta$-decay of both the ground state and isomer of $^{186}$Hg to $^{186}$Au's excited states was analyzed using a high-resolution magnetic storage ring. The data revealed that $^{186}$Hg's ground state predominantly decays to the $7/2^+$ state, while the $5/2^+$ state is the primary decay mode of the $^{186}$Hg isomer. The findings are in line with nuclear structure predictions. The $^{186}$Hg isomer's unusually long half-life is attributed to its $7/2^+$ configuration, which hinders $\beta$-decay to the $^{186}$Au's known low-lying states. The $^{186}$Hg isomer serves as an ideal source for studying $^{186}$Au's $\gamma$ transitions.

We explore a unified framework that integrates both the dark matter field and lepton generation, with Drellin process acting as the primary dark matter producer. A large scalar field, whose vacuum expectation value sets the dark matter density, also determines the dark matter mass. In contrast, a light sterile neutrino is generated through the standard Dira potential, also influenced by the scalar field's vacuum expectation value. A phase space distribution analysis is carried out to calculate the dark matter and light neutrino masses as well as the baryon density. A detailed examination of these results is provided within this framework.

This study introduces a novel control method that enables the simultaneous acquisition of multiple skills using limited information. The skills can be grouped into two categories: (a) skills with a singular objective, such as navigation to a specific destination, and (b) skills with multiple objectives, like goal-oriented movement accompanied by obstacle avoidance. The approach is demonstrated on a 14-degree-of-freedom humanoid robot capable of reaching, swimming, walking, and flying. The underlying technique, referred to as RL3V, employs reinforcement learning, specifically the Continuous Control with Hindsight (CC-HIT) algorithm, and relies on the incorporation of relevant external data and side information. The presence of abundant external data facilitates learning, while the side information helps the robot generalize its abilities. The approach is evaluated by conducting experiments on the X-100 robot, a versatile 14-degree-of-freedom humanoid robot, and the results demonstrate that CC-HIT can successfully master all four skills after a single trial. Furthermore, the approach exhibits the capability to adapt to unforeseen scenarios, such as changes in the environment, variations in side information, and shifts in task requirements.
We've found and computed a broad set of Ward identities, which are valid for the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory's correlation functions.

In the realm of generative adversarial networks (GANs), incorporating prior knowledge from specific tasks can be beneficial. A previous study, called Relation GAN, introduced an encoder-decoder architecture with multiple interconnected components, using shared latent space, to generate conditioned images. This work builds upon that by developing an alternative approach, employing triplet loss instead of cross-entropy, to achieve the same goal. By utilizing triplet loss, our proposed model, Relation Triplet GAN, generates images that align with the prior distribution of natural images, as opposed to relying on cross-entropy, which may lead to an improper prior. This improvement is demonstrated through extensive evaluations on diverse datasets, including DAVIS, LSUN Church, and DAVIS, where our model achieves superior results.

The typical quantum key distribution method employs single photons, yet it is restricted by the Shot Noise limit in terms of transmission distance. The twin-field QKD overcomes this by utilizing a more complex interference measurement method, however it requires precise phase synchronization between distant parties. A novel TFQKD protocol is presented which doesn't rely on phase synchronization, instead using random bit encoding and relying on photon number squeezing for secure key generation, even in the presence of photon number squeezing.

Let G be a finite abelian group and H be one of the following spaces: the Drinfeld upper half plane, Drinfeld half plane, or the polydisk. The article identifies the Toeplitz algebra of the Fock or Hardy space on G with respect to a parameter λ or φ, and expresses it as an extension of the Cuntz-Krieger or Cuntz algebra over G, or directly as a product of the corresponding Drinfeld Toeplitz algebras, depending on the parameter's nature. Furthermore, the article characterizes the Toeplitz algebra of Hardy or Fock space on G as an extension of the Toeplitz algebra of the corresponding space on a point, involving a free product of certain UHF algebras or a maximal torus of a unitary group.

Current research on open vocabulary object detection is hindered by a lack of precise annotations in training data, typically represented by coarse class labels accompanied by image-level bounding boxes. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method, pseudo bounding-box detection, which generates refined bounding boxes from image data using a reference model. This technique is built upon the principles of progressive refinement and boundary optimization. By integrating pseudo bounding-box detection into training, our approach significantly enhances the accuracy of final models. Moreover, our method demonstrates improved detection performance on fine-grained challenges such as CUB200 and CarS, surpassing state-of-the-art results.

The Rho Ophiuchus molecular cloud is a well-studied region of star formation, particularly around the T Tauri star S1. Our work, using a 1.5-meter telescope, reveals the PDR tracers S8 and S12 surrounding S1, which were previously undetected. The PDRs surrounding S1 show a 1000 AU separation and a 25 km/second expansion velocity, which is consistent with previous observations. The PDRs' gas temperature and density are also measured at 100 K and 10 to the 5th power cm to the -3, respectively. A 300 AU wide and 50 AU high ionized region surrounds the PDRs, with the PDRs themselves being 50 AU wide and 200 AU high. Our findings suggest that the PDRs' formation is due to the photoevaporation of a shell by S1, which is a 20 solar mass B star.

Transformer-based models have significantly advanced natural language processing, and veracity prediction, a specialized task, has recently garnered attention. Although NLP has seen rapid growth, practical applications of machine learning remain limited, and veracity prediction, encompassing both fact-checking and document validation, represents a crucial area of study. This survey explores veracity prediction using transformer-based models, covering its definition, the four primary classification types, foundational knowledge for NLP and fact-checking, data sources, evaluation methods, and challenges. We also outline future directions and provide a comprehensive overview of existing approaches to veracity prediction, aiming to facilitate the development of models and inform the choices of practitioners.

Mortality forecasting models based on mortality laws are being increasingly factored into asset-liability management and insurance risk models. There's ongoing debate about the usefulness of factoring in model components - whether the factor model structure provides an advantage over a single-equation framework. This paper investigates this issue, using a simple model with one observation per year of a single age group, and demonstrates that: (i) a factor model with time-varying factor loadings offers the same level of precision as the single-equation framework; (ii) a factor model with time-invariant factor loadings provides a significant precision advantage over the single-equation framework. These results are supported by numerical simulations and empirical evidence from real-world data, and a review of existing factored models reveals that they typically incorporate time-invariant factor loadings.

Research on Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has yielded impressive results, yet it remains an intricate and computationally demanding process that necessitates significant development efforts. To address this challenge, existing studies have sought to mitigate NAS's complexity by categorizing architectures into distinct types to facilitate search within specific subsets. Nevertheless, these efforts have not thoroughly examined the sources of complexity nor assessed the effectiveness of their proposed subsets. In an attempt to address these shortcomings, this study aims to (1) identify the primary factors contributing to NAS's complexity and (2) develop strategies to reduce these factors. To this end, this research investigates how variations in design constraints, search objectives, and database subsets impact NAS's complexity and performance, and subsequently, this study proposes two methods to decrease NAS's complexity. Two of these methods involve (1) leveraging transferability to limit search to previously explored architectures, and (2) strategically distributing design constraints to reduce their search space. Experimental results demonstrate that these strategies can effectively reduce the number of candidate architectures by 50% and 10% respectively, while maintaining competitive performance on ImageNet.

This paper presents an overview of time series transformation techniques using feature extraction, which are essential for both statistical and machine learning analysis.. These methods, implemented within the theft package in R, enable time series comparison through a set of characteristic features. Three main classes of transformations are explored: those based on signal processing, distance measures, and correlation coefficients. Additionally, we demonstrate how to apply these techniques to detect copycat behavior in sports, utilizing football data as a test case.

We introduce a precise criterion for the completeness of a geodesic chart in a CAT(0) space, relying on a finite, verifiable condition regarding the behavior of sequences approaching zero thickness. This criterion ensures that a geodesic chart extension can be achieved. Additionally, a necessary and sufficient condition for the extension of a geodesic chart is established when the space has finite radius. Our analysis also includes a characterization of the tangent cones at boundary points within a geodesically complete CAT(0) space.

Assessing the reliability of translators is crucial in the context of translating medical texts, where inaccuracies can have significant consequences. To address this issue, a Bayesian approach has been developed to evaluate translator reliability based on their ability to identify errors in the source text during the translating process. Through simulated experiments, this method has demonstrated satisfactory results in assessing translator reliability.

The relationship between energy deposition and various properties of a body, such as its density and nuclear cross sections, has been widely studied in both inelastic neutron scattering and optical absorption. The energy deposited by a body's response to these interactions can be broken down into various channels, and we can use sum rules to establish a fundamental connection between the total energy deposition and the distribution of its weight across these channels. These sum rules can be applied to any scattering process, and we explore their implications for both weak and strong scattering regimes. We also examine how the distribution of energy deposition among different eigenchannels changes as a function of energy, using computational models for hydrogen and water.

In the realm of neural networks, the 'pruning' technique has gained significant traction for its ability to enhance the efficiency of trained networks. A recent paper investigates the effects of pruning on ReLU networks, specifically examining whether the architecture of the network (fully connected vs convolutional) impacts performance after pruning. The study reveals that pruning can help identify essential network components, much like a lottery ticket, and that convolutional networks have distinct advantages over fully connected networks in this context. The research also explores the characteristics of influential subnetworks and highlights the importance of maintaining sparsity throughout the network's layers to preserve performance.

In many countries, particularly in the United States, individuals purchase lottery tickets regularly, despite odds of winning being extremely low.  Previous studies have found that a significant number of people find the lottery enjoyable, and surprisingly, a certain level of loss is often preferred.  Building on this concept, our study examines anticipations of losses and gains by analyzing the structure of the lottery and exploring how its features influence anticipated profits.  We develop a method to calculate anticipations using the structure-preserving price transformation and apply it to analyze the most common US lotteries.  Results indicate that people who buy lottery tickets aim to win jackpots at least twice the cost of the ticket, and our study shows that an optimal price for a lottery ticket exists when the price is less than $1, allowing for a loss of around 50%, and exists when the ticket is less than $10, allowing for a loss of around 90%.  Furthermore, our study shows that an optimal time to buy a lottery ticket exists when the ticket is sold and provides insights into how the seller can maximize the anticipations by adjusting the number of tickets, jackpots, and costs.

The value of the six-loop anomalous dimension for the $\phi^Q$ operator within the $O(N)$ symmetric model has been determined, which allows for the calculation to the first order of the $1/Q$ expansion of its corresponding anomalous exponent $\gamma_{0, N}^{(Q)}$. This is expressed as $\gamma_{0, N}^{(Q)} = \gamma_\varphi^{(Q, 1/\epsilon)} + c_1/Q + O(1/Q^2)$, where $\gamma_\varphi$ denotes the anomalous dimension of a single field $\phi$. This formula is further refined by incorporating the known five-loop expression for $\gamma_\phi$. As a result, this allows us to obtain critical exponents to higher precision for the case of quasi-one-dimensional systems, and to generate additional data points for the $1/\epsilon$ expansion of the critical exponents.

Valley polarization is a crucial property in two-dimensional materials, but it is often compromised by electron-phonon interactions.
